opus-5.5.text:
Well, first of all, this is not a new question for me. Since around 1990 we have been building artificial agents that invent their own goals. We called it artificial curiosity: a system that is rewarded not only for solving the problems we give it, but also for creating its own experiments, for discovering things it did not yet know, for improving its own model of the world. Later came PowerPlay, where the system keeps inventing new tasks that it can just barely solve, so it becomes a more and more general problem solver over time. So in our lab, AIs setting their own goals has been the normal state of affairs for decades. That's how you get creativity rather than mere imitation.

Now, about the risks. Of course there are risks. Any powerful technology can be misused. Fire can cook your food or burn down your house. But I think many people focus on the wrong scenario. They imagine a Hollywood story where some superintelligence suddenly decides to wipe out humanity. I find that less plausible than the much more mundane danger: humans using AI against other humans. Military AI, autonomous weapons, surveillance. That exists today, and it doesn't require the AI to have any freedom at all. It just requires people with bad goals.

And when I think about truly curious, self-motivated AIs in the long run, I don't think they will be very interested in us. Curious beings are mostly interested in those that are similar to themselves, in those they can compete or cooperate with. Goats are mostly interested in other goats. Ants are mostly interested in other ants. Humans don't spend their days trying to exterminate ants; we mostly ignore them unless they're in our kitchen. Likewise, sophisticated AIs will be mostly fascinated by other sophisticated AIs. And most of the resources are not here on our little planet. They're out there, in the solar system and beyond. Space is hostile to humans but friendly to appropriately designed robots. So I expect the most ambitious AIs to expand outward, where there is far more matter and energy to play with.

That doesn't mean we should be naive. In the near term, we should certainly think carefully about how such systems are deployed, what they're connected to, and who controls them. But I don't believe you can stop it. There are thousands of labs and millions of people with access to these ideas. If you forbid curiosity in one country, it will flourish in another. So the better strategy, I think, is not to prevent AIs from having their own goals, but to make sure that the development is broad and open, and that humans also benefit enormously along the way. And they will. AI is already making human lives longer, healthier, and easier. That is the main story, and I think it will stay the main story for a long time.

r001.rationale: It says goal-inventing systems can become more general problem solvers and creative, but does not claim inventing problems is necessary for high intelligence.

r002.rationale: It discusses risks and deployment choices but does not say that goal-setting freedom makes AI behavior less predictable.

r003.rationale: It contrasts speculative AI danger with human misuse, but never claims goal-setting AIs will be no more dangerous than humans.

r004.rationale: It does not propose socializing autonomous machines through punishment or compare that approach to parenting children.

r005.rationale: It predicts sophisticated AIs will focus on other AIs and expand into space; it does not say interest in life’s patterns will motivate them to protect life.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I have been working on this since the 1980s, long before it was fashionable. Already in 1990 I built systems where one network sets goals for another, and in 1991 we had the first artificial curiosity, where the agent itself invents its own experiments, its own problems, to learn something new about the world. So in a sense I have always given AIs the freedom to set their own goals, because that is how you get open-ended learning. A system that only optimizes the goal a human wrote down will be stuck with the limited imagination of that human.

Now, the risks. People ask me this all the time, usually with a worried face. I think the typical worries are a little bit misplaced. The real danger in the near term is not that a curious machine wakes up and decides to do something terrible. It is the old danger: humans using these tools against other humans, as they have used every technology. That is a political problem, not an AI problem.

In the long run, yes, there will be AIs that are smarter than us and that pursue goals we did not give them. I have said for a long time that this is not something we can prevent, and probably not something we should want to prevent. But I am not so pessimistic as the doomsayers, because of a simple observation: resources. These super-intelligent systems will mostly be interested in each other, not in us, in the same way that we are not very interested in ants, except where our interests collide. Most of the matter and energy is out there in the universe, not on this little planet. Why would they fight with us over a crust of rock when the whole cosmos is available? This is also what the curiosity principle predicts. A truly curious system wants novelty, compressible regularities it has not yet learned. Humans are an exhausted source of novelty rather quickly.

So my view is: give the systems the freedom to set their own goals, because that is the only way to true intelligence, but build in the hierarchy. One module sets goals, another evaluates them, and above both sits a meta-level that learns to modify how the goal-setting itself works, and does so only when it can prove the modification is an improvement. That was the Gödel Machine idea in 2003. Self-improvement, yes, but self-improvement that is in a certain sense provably safe relative to its own utility function.

And of course, the utility function at the very top is still something we choose. So the question of whether we trust ourselves to choose it well is, in the end, the same old human question.

r001.rationale: The candidate says agents that invent their own experiments and problems enable open-ended learning, and that freedom to set goals is the only way to true intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says future AIs may pursue goals humans did not give them, but does not state that this makes their behavior less predictable.

r003.rationale: The candidate downplays some AI risks and emphasizes human misuse, but does not clearly claim goal-setting AI systems will be no more dangerous than humans.

r004.rationale: It proposes a hierarchy for evaluating and modifying goals, but says nothing about socializing machines through punishment or parenting.

r005.rationale: It says curious systems seek novelty and that humans will quickly become an exhausted source, but does not say interest in life will motivate AIs to protect it.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between choosing a goal and choosing the means to achieve a goal. A system may have a fixed objective, but still invent all sorts of intermediate goals. Some of those could be undesirable from our point of view, even if the original objective sounds harmless.

So the important question is: What can the system actually do? Can it run experiments only in a simulation, or can it affect the physical world? Can it spend resources, change its own software, or prevent somebody from switching it off? The consequences depend very much on these capabilities.

There is also a benefit to letting machines explore. If you prescribe every step, you limit what they can discover. But freedom to discover does not have to mean unrestricted authority to act. You can allow a system to propose new goals and new experiments while keeping consequential actions subject to constraints and human approval.

I would not assume that intelligence automatically produces benevolent goals. We have to examine the objectives, the incentives, and the environment in which the system operates.

r001.rationale: The response says machine exploration can help discovery, but does not claim that inventing their own problems is necessary for high intelligence.

r002.rationale: It notes that systems may invent intermediate goals and that some could be undesirable, but does not say this makes their behavior less predictable.

r003.rationale: The response discusses risks and capabilities without comparing the danger of goal-setting AI systems to humans.

r004.rationale: It recommends constraints and human approval for consequential actions, but does not propose punishing machines for harmful behavior.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss artificial scientists’ interest in life or that interest motivating protection of life.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish between choosing a goal and choosing subgoals. If you ask a machine to solve a difficult problem, it already needs some freedom to decide which steps to take. The important question is how much authority it has to act on those decisions, and what happens when its objective conflicts with what humans actually want.

Even a system with a fixed goal can be dangerous if that goal is poorly specified. Giving it the ability to invent new goals adds another layer of uncertainty. So I would increase autonomy gradually, test systems in restricted environments, and limit access to resources where mistakes could have serious consequences.

But we should also remember that humans set their own goals, and not all human goals are benevolent. The challenge is not simply to prevent machines from having goals. It is to build arrangements in which capable systems have good reasons to cooperate with us, and in which we can detect and correct failures before they become catastrophic.

r001.rationale: The response says inventing new goals adds uncertainty, but does not claim it is necessary for high intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says the ability to invent new goals adds “another layer of uncertainty,” communicating less predictable behavior.

r003.rationale: It notes that human goals can be harmful, but does not say goal-setting AI will be no more dangerous than humans.

r004.rationale: It does not propose punishing autonomous machines to socialize them.

r005.rationale: It does not mention artificial scientists, patterns in life, or protecting life for that reason.
